doc.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: New England Conservatory, bass studies, choir and Newton High School
summary: His conservatory studies, learning bass in junior high, the pop department, choral training and the adventurous high school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: The New England Conservatory, you went there and you played bass and piano?

The first year I was a piano major and a bass minor, and I was studying with Georges Muller on bass, who was the first bassist with the Boston Symphony, and Roland Nadeau on piano. I had taught myself how to read bass music and how to play the instrument because in junior high school there were eight pianists that wanted to play and the band director said, “How would you like to play one of those?” And I said, “Fine.” So I became a bass player. And I did that for ten years including amateur symphony work. So it probably contributes to my love for strings a lot. I adore strings. And it probably led directly to the formation of my group the Cello Quartet, which was in the 70s.
Yeah I want to talk about that but down the line just a little bit. You played, your studies in the conservatory were mostly of a classical nature?
Well they were except at that time we had a pop department. And a pop department at that time meant a jazz department.
Ahh. That’s an important statement. I mean from a historical standpoint. Pop music was jazz, or jazz tinged.

It was much more jazz oriented at that time. Just like what’s jazz? I mean it’s — the definition of jazz now has gotten so absurd that there are players that are supposedly qualified as jazz players that aren’t jazz players at all. And their music isn’t jazz. We don’t need to go into that. There are too many of them. But I stayed in the Conservatory for two years. The second year I was a composition major with Jed Cooke, and a piano minor. And I kept studying bass, and I had choir. Choral was conducted by a woman named Cooke deVaron. And I had eleven years of choral training, which is probably the best ear training that anyone could ever have. But I love singing. We sang with the Boston Symphony and all the major requiems plus Honegger, the “Honegger Christmas Cantata” — it’s one of the greatest pieces ever written for me. And in high school we played Menotti’s “Amahl and the Night Visitors” and we had a very adventurous high school. We had two years of theory, college credit. And an orchestra under Don March
